To fix (3)

To fix Marginal Significance

What we found

You described 5 effects with terms related to ‘marginally significant’.

Show details

You described effects with terms related to ‘marginally significant’. If p values above 0.05 are interpreted as an effect, you inflate the alpha level, and increase the Type 1 error rate. If a p value is higher than the prespecified alpha level, it should be interpreted as a non-significant result.

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 19 imprecise p values out of 31 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

To check (5)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 25 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

To check Codebook Check

What we found

We found no codebook or README documentation for the 510 extracted data columns.

Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 9 codebook/README/label sources and 510 data columns across 25 files.

No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.

Duplicated Column Names

  • Duplicated column names in sim_results.csv. 1 column name appears more than once (worst: V1×2), so 2 of the file’s 36 columns share a name with another. This usually means a survey loop/merge exported repeated blocks without numbering each iteration; the repeats cannot be told apart and can only be documented once. Consider re-exporting with per-iteration column names.

Archive Files

The following files are not ZIP archives: metamixr_0.1.0.tar.gz. We recommend the .zip format for archives: only ZIP stores its file listing in a way that lets a tool inspect the contents without downloading the whole archive, so a .zip is more discoverable and re-usable than a .7z, .rar, .tar or .tar.gz.

Unclassified Files

2 files are of a kind metacheck does not know, so they are not counted as data, code or documentation: configure, configure.win. This is no problem in itself.

File Naming

File names should be machine-parseable: no spaces or special characters, and every file should be classifiable by name or extension. We found 1 naming problem that should be fixed, and 36 files with a naming suggestion (not required, but a good habit).

Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.

Missing Files

All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 4 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 510 columns across 25 data files.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 25 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A package could not be installed.

  • bias_simscript_freq_methods_twosided.R needs metamix.
  • bias_simscript_freq_methods.R needs metamix.
  • nobias_simscript.R needs metamix.
  • visualize_low_tau_mix.R needs metamix.

metamix is not on CRAN, and your code does not say where it comes from. If it comes from GitHub or Bioconductor, install it at the top of the script, or name the command in the README, for example remotes::install_github(“user/metamix”) or BiocManager::install(“metamix”), with the version you used.

A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.

  • nudging_remove1.5+wansink.Rmd
  • run_robustness.R
  • failure_sim.R

State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting.

File paths

21 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: run_sim_failure.R to simulation/simulation3/simulation_scripts/run_sim_failure.R (in failure_sim.R); posterior_model_probs.csv to results/posterior_model_probs.csv (in make_latex_tables.R); estimates_M3.csv to results/estimates_M3.csv (in make_latex_tables.R); jackknife_allocation_agreement.csv to results/jackknife_allocation_agreement.csv (in make_latex_tables.R); data_used.rds to results/data_used.rds (in summarise_robustness.R); ../run_sim.R to simulation/simulation2/simulation_scripts/run_sim.R (in two_step0505.R); ../run_sim.R to simulation/simulation2/simulation_scripts/run_sim.R (in two_step052.R); ../run_sim.R to simulation/simulation2/simulation_scripts/run_sim.R (in two_step205.R); ../run_sim.R to simulation/simulation2/simulation_scripts/run_sim.R (in two_step22.R); ../run_sim_two_sided.R to simulation/simulation2/simulation_scripts/run_sim_two_sided.R (in two_sided0505.R), and 11 more. The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. The code reads files that are only inside robustness.zip, two_step.zip, two_sided.zip, no_bias.zip, one_step.zip, package/metamixr_0.1.0.tar.gz, and no script unpacks them. We unpacked them in their folder before the run. So that others can run the code as deposited, start the code with a line that unpacks them (such as unzip("robustness.zip") in R), or upload the files unpacked. 5 data paths were built at runtime with sprintf()/paste()/file.path() instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author’s own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 36 scripts: 7 ran without error, 3 errored, 3 timed out, 4 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 3 were run by another script with source(). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 3 scripts could not be tried, because a file they need was not downloaded: postprobs_percell.R, visualize_sim_results.R, percell_pb_detection_median.R. They are not counted as scripts that did not reproduce. The file: simulation/simulation2/results/merged_metamix_results_rerun.csv (115.7 MB); files over 100 MB are not downloaded.

>   cl <- cutree(hclust(dist(cm, method = "maximum"), method = "complete"), h = spread_threshold)
>   med <- function(p, chains) median(arr[, chains, p])
>   centre <- function(chains) {
>     th <- sapply(seq_len(M), function(m) med(sprintf("theta[%d]", m), chains))
>     out <- list(mu1    = med("mu1", chains),
>                 mu_gap = if (M > 1) sapply(seq_len(M - 1), function(m) med(sprintf("mu_gap[%d]", m), chains)) else numeric(0),
>                 tau    = sapply(seq_len(M), function(m) med(sprintf("tau[%d]", m), chains)),
>                 theta  = th / sum(th))
>     if (has_par(fit, "omega_raw")) {
>       om <- sapply(seq_len(length(steps) + 1), function(k) med(sprintf("omega_raw[%d]", k), chains))
>       out$omega_raw <- om / sum(om)
>     }
>     out
>   }
>   groups <- sort(unique(cl))
>   basins <- lapply(groups, function(g) {
>     chains <- which(cl == g)
>     list(centre = centre(chains), chains = chains, c_logtau = mean(cm[chains, mstar]))
>   })
>   basins <- basins[order(sapply(basins, `[[`, "c_logtau"))]
>   names(basins) <- paste0("b", seq_along(basins))
>   list(basins = basins, mstar = mstar, centres = sapply(basins, `[[`, "c_logtau"))
> }
> make_inits <- function(centre, n_chains, jitter = 0.05) {
>   lapply(seq_len(n_chains), function(i) {
>     j  <- function(x) if (length(x)) x * exp(rnorm(length(x), 0, jitter)) else x
>     th <- j(centre$theta)
>     out <- list(mu1    = centre$mu1 + rnorm(1, 0, jitter * max(abs(centre$mu1), 0.01)),
>                 mu_gap = as.array(j(centre$mu_gap)),
>                 tau    = as.array(j(centre$tau)),
>                 theta  = as.array(th / sum(th)))
>     if (!is.null(centre$omega_raw)) { om <- j(centre$omega_raw); out$omega_raw <- as.array(om / sum(om)) }
>     out
>   })
> }
> nearest_basin <- function(values, centres) names(centres)[apply(abs(outer(values, centres, "-")), 1, which.min)]
> basin_converged <- function(fit, M, mstar, b, centres) {
>   cm <- chain_log_tau(fit, M)[, mstar]
>   cv <- conv(fit)
>   all(nearest_basin(cm, centres) == b) && cv[["max_rhat"]] < rhat_flag
> }
> fit_one <- function(t) {
>   id  <- task_id(t)
>   out <- file.path(out_dir, paste0(id, ".rds"))
>   if (file.exists(out)) return(id)   # finished fits are skipped on a rerun
>   y <- y_all[t$keep]; s <- sd_all[t$keep]
>   seed <- seed_base + t$rep * 100 + t$M
>   ref  <- is_ref(t)
>   t0 <- Sys.time()
> 
>   ## ---- STAGE A: default random inits, full length ----
>   fitA <- fit_model(t, c(model_args(t, y, s, chains = if (ref) ref_chains else var_chains,
>                                     cores = if (ref) n_cores else 1), list(seed = seed)))
>   bsA  <- bridge_sampler(fitA, silent = TRUE)
>   cvA  <- conv(fitA)
>   flagged <- is_flagged(cvA)
>   fit <- fitA; bs <- bsA; used_basin <- "single"; used_conv <- !flagged
>   P_used <- 1; n_basins <- 1L; basin_tab <- NULL
>   stageB_note <- if (!flagged) "converged directly (single mode)" else "flagged; NON-converged (no mode resolution for single-component models)"
> 
>   ## ---- STAGE B: basins + per-basin refits for flagged models ----
>   if (flagged && t$M >= 2) {
>     mi <- extract_basins(fitA, t$M)
>     if (is.null(mi)) {
>       stageB_note <- "flagged; chains not mode-separated (slow mixing) -> non-converged"
>     } else {
>       set.seed(seed)
>       bns   <- names(mi$basins)
>       bfits <- lapply(bns, function(b) fit_model(t, c(model_args(t, y, s, chains = basin_chains, cores = if (ref) n_cores else 1),
>                                                       list(init = make_inits(mi$basins[[b]]$centre, basin_chains), seed = seed + match(b, bns)))))
>       bbs   <- lapply(bfits, function(f) tryCatch(bridge_sampler(f, silent = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL))
>       z     <- setNames(sapply(bbs, function(m) if (is.null(m)) NA_real_ else m$logml), bns)
>       bconv <- setNames(sapply(seq_along(bns), function(i) basin_converged(bfits[[i]], t$M, mi$mstar, bns[i], mi$centres)), bns)
>       zf    <- replace(z, !is.finite(z), -Inf)
>       P     <- exp(zf - max(zf)) / sum(exp(zf - max(zf)))
>       cand  <- bns[bconv & is.finite(z)]
>       ## STAGE C: evidence = best CONVERGED basin; model converged iff that basin dominates
>       sel   <- if (length(cand)) cand[which.max(z[cand])] else names(which.max(zf))
>       fit <- bfits[[match(sel, bns)]]; bs <- bbs[[match(sel, bns)]]
>       used_basin <- sel; used_conv <- isTRUE(bconv[[sel]]); P_used <- P[[sel]]; n_basins <- length(bns)
>       basin_tab <- data.frame(basin = bns, c_logtau = round(mi$centres, 3), logml = z, P = round(P, 4),
>                               converged = bconv, used = bns == sel, row.names = NULL)
>       stageB_note <- if (used_conv && P_used > dom_threshold) {
>         if (all(bconv)) "multimodal; resolved, best converged mode used"
>         else "multimodal; used basin clean and dominant (a negligible-mass basin did not converge)"
>       } else "NON-converged: used basin failed to mix or does not clearly dominate -> evidence unreliable"
>     }
>   }
>   converged <- used_conv && P_used > dom_threshold && !is.null(bs)
>   fit_min <- as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "mins"))
> 
>   ## ---- summaries from the used fit ----
>   em <- if (is.null(bs)) list(re2 = NA, cv = NA) else error_measures(bs)
>   sm <- rstan::summary(fit, pars = intersect(sum_pars, fit@model_pars))$summary[, c("mean", "2.5%", "97.5%", "n_eff", "Rhat"), drop = FALSE]
>   cv <- conv(fit)
>   res <- list(
>     id = id, analysis = t$analysis, label = t$label, type = t$type, rep = t$rep, M = t$M,
>     keep = t$keep, K = length(y), prior = t$prior, proc_version = proc_version,
>     logml = if (is.null(bs)) NA_real_ else bs$logml, bridge_re2 = em$re2, bridge_cv = em$cv,
>     summary = sm, max_rhat = cv[["max_rhat"]], min_ess = cv[["min_ess"]], divergences = cv[["divergences"]],
>     alloc = matrix(colMeans(as.matrix(fit, pars = "posterior_probs")), nrow = length(y), ncol = t$M),
>     fit_min = fit_min,
>     ## multimodality record
>     stageA = list(chains = if (ref) ref_chains else var_chains, max_rhat = cvA[["max_rhat"]], min_ess = cvA[["min_ess"]],

>                   chain_log_tau = chain_log_tau(fitA, t$M)),
>     flagged = flagged, n_basins = n_basins, basins = basin_tab, used_basin = used_basin,
>     used_conv = used_conv, P_used = P_used, converged = converged, note = stageB_note
>   )
>   saveRDS(res, out)
>   id
> }

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

The paper does not appear to report data about individual people or animals (we found: a review or meta-analysis named in the title or abstract; simulations; theorems or proofs), so we do not expect an ethics statement.

We based this on:

The R-package for fitting meta-analytic mixture models is available on CRAN (install.packages(“metamixr”)) and at https://github.com/MaxMaier42/metamix and additional guidance on the package can be found at https://maxmaier42.github.io/metamix/.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
