Simulation 3: Boundary Conditions of Meta-Analytic Mixture Modelling

Simulation Setup

Simulation 3 examines three plausible departures from the conditions in Simulations 1 and 2 that would likely reduce the performance of meta-analytic mixture modelling or where assumptions are violated: 1.

Few primary studies: K = 30 instead of 100, for both M = 1 & M = 2.

2. Unequal mixing weights: θ = (0.10, 0.90) instead of (0.5, 0.5), so the null component contains on average only 10 studies.

3. Non-normal true effects: a single lognormal population with mean 0.5 and standard deviation 0.4 (skewness ≈ 2.9) with effect sizes bounded between -2 and 2 to avoid extreme outliers.

Each of these parameters was varied one at a time using the Simulation 2 setting with K = 100 primary studies, two components with means 0 and 0.5, τ = 0.05 in both mixture components as starting point. Each of the six resulting cells was crossed with the four publication processes of Simulation 2 and repeated 336 times.

Results

Publication Bias. One benefit of the mixture modelling is that it may improve publication bias detection even when data are not generated from a mixture of normals, as it can flexibly approximate other types of distributions. Fitting a mixture model indeed considerably improves publication bias detection when data are in fact generated from a log-normal distribution (Figure 8). MetaMix retains a relatively low false positive rate (albeit a slightly higher one than when data are generated from a mixture of normals), while at the same time reliably detecting publication bias when it is present. Other methods perform worse than MetaMix and either have high false positive rates or low power to detect publication bias. This result shows that mixtures are useful as a flexible approximating device to improve inferences about publication bias, even when the data-generating process is not a mixture.

Example: Exploring the Heterogeneity of Nudging

In this section, I illustrate how MetaMix can be used to explore the heterogeneity of nudging. Nudging describes changing the choice environment (e.g., setting a default option or making one option more salient) in order to steer behaviour without restricting options or altering incentives. I applied MetaMix to a large meta-analysis on nudging [28], comprising more than 440 effect sizes from more than 200 studies. Mertens et al. [28] argued that choice architecture (i.e., nudging) interventions overall promote behaviour change (d = .43). However, reanalyses of the paper showed that this overall effect disappears when adjusting for publication bias [64, 65]. The paper by Mertens and colleagues and the associated commentaries sparked discussion about the meaning of the overall effect of nudges and the importance of developing a deeper understanding of the heterogeneity of behaviour change interventions [66] [67] [68]. I therefore revisited this dataset using the meta-analytic mixture modelling methods developed in this paper. Because of limitations in the underlying data (see e.g., [69]), this analysis should be considered mostly as an illustration of the new method rather than a definitive account of which types of nudges are effective. 7 7 I removed all effect sizes d > 1.5 due to evidence of coding errors for some of the very large effect sizes [69] and all studies that were coauthored by Brian Wansink, as he had been involved in research I applied both random-effects mixtures without publication bias adjustment and mixtures of selection models with cutoffs at p = .5 and p = .975.8 Table 1 shows the posterior model probabilities of models with and without publication bias adjustment and with different numbers of mixture components.

The posterior model probability was roughly equally split between 3 and 4 component mixtures assuming publication bias.

For each cluster, I estimated a mixing weight in terms of the proportion of observed studies (i.e., after selection) and a mixing weight in terms of the proportion of all studies (i.e., before selection) in that component. Finally, an important consideration when fitting mixture models is the stability of the recovered solution. Because mixtures are flexible approximating devices, different configurations of components may describe the same data similarly well. A prerequisite for interpreting mixture components is therefore that the solution is stable under small changes to the data and to the modelling choices. To assess this, I first refitted each model with 16 chains and random starting values to assess possible posterior multimodality. Only the two-component selection model was multimodal, and its dominant mode (posterior probability 0.999) reproduced the estimate reported here (see also https://maxmaier42.github.io/metamix/articles/multimodality.html). Second, I refitted the models after randomly removing 10% of the effect sizes and under a range of alternative prior specifications (Appendix F). The recovered mixture was robust across these variations: the cluster means, mixing weights, and study allocations changed little with the largest effect being that tighter priors on the heterogeneity lead to a larger µ 3 (µ3 = 0.93 [0.42, 1.19] under τ ∼ Normal + (0, 0.1) versus 0.59 [0.18, 1.07] under τ ∼ Normal + (0, 0.5)). Further, the uncertainty about the number of components remained confined to the choice between three and four clusters; however, the choice between the two did vary across the replicates with some of them strongly favouring a four cluster solution, which splits the first component into two (see Appendix F).

Discussion

Applications of meta-analysis have long relied on the untested assumption that all effect sizes follow a single normal distribution. In this paper, I showed that if wrong, this assumption can seriously compromise meta-analytic inferences, in particular in the presence of publication bias. To mitigate this issue, I propose meta-analytic mixture modelling (MetaMix), which models meta-analytic effect sizes as a mixture of several normal distributions. I combine Bayesian meta-analytic mixture models with selection models to correct for publication bias and provide them in the metamixr R-package.

In the example provided in this paper, I used existing, coded moderators to characterize the mixture components. While this is a pragmatic way of interpreting mixture components, especially for reanalyses of secondary data, I anticipate that researchers with domain expertise can consider various additional factors that cannot easily be captured using standard moderator analysis. In particular, meta-analysts knowledgeable of the primary literature included in the meta-analysis can re-read the studies with highest posterior probability of being in a specific cluster. This will allow cluster descriptions based on richer theoretical insights than coded moderators, which are often constrained to relatively high-level, easy-to-code variables that apply to all primary studies [72].

Theoretical knowledge of the domain area under consideration is therefore crucial in meta-analytic mixture modelling in order to interpret the identified clusters. Further, cluster allocation can be analyzed using machine learning techniques, such as random forest, and associated interpretability techniques, such as permutation importance, to recover the importance of different predictors [73]. This allows researchers to account for more complex interactions and nonlinear relationships that would be difficult to accommodate in classical moderator analysis.

I expect meta-analytic mixture modelling to be most suitable for relatively large meta-analyses with broader inclusion criteria, as it is more likely that the data indeed arise from a mixture process with distinct components in these types of meta-analyses. When the distance between cluster means is small relative to the amount of heterogeneity, the number of clusters tends to be underestimated as the distribution of effect sizes is strongly merged (see Figure B1). However, when the presence of multiple clusters is not detected, applying MetaMix has no downsides compared to applying a random-effects model directly, while it has considerable upsides when multiple clusters are detected.

Similarly, when the primary sample sizes are small, some studies may not be clearly assigned to any one mixture component. In particular, studies with effect size estimates between component means often have similar probability of belonging to the two closest components. To mitigate this issue, I recommend focusing on the studies most diagnostic of each cluster when interpreting the mixture components (which will often also be the ones with the largest sample size). In the example, I visualized studies with a probability larger 50% of corresponding to a cluster.

Because mixtures are highly flexible in how they approximate a distribution, different configurations of components can describe the same data similarly well, and a solution that depends on the particular prior or on a handful of studies should not be interpreted. Researchers should therefore assess the robustness of a fitted mixture before interpreting it. Useful checks include refitting the models under alternative prior specifications, refitting after randomly removing a small proportion of studies and examining whether the number of components, the component estimates, and the allocation of studies to components remain stable, as illustrated for the nudging example above.

Importantly, stability of the recovered components is a necessary condition for giving them a substantive interpretation, but it is not a sufficient one, as discussed in the next section.

What Do Mixture Components Represent?

Like all statistical methods, meta-analytic mixture modelling relies on assumptions.

Although introducing a mixture allows for a more flexible data-generating process than a single normal distribution, it still assumes that effect sizes within each latent cluster are normally distributed, an assumption that is plausible given that the normal distribution is the maximum entropy distribution for a specified mean and variance. When the underlying distribution is non-normal, a finite mixture of normals usually provides a better approximation of the data-generating process than a single normal. However, when mixtures are used primarily as approximating devices, researchers should be cautious about assigning substantive or theoretical interpretations to the resulting clusters. Given that it is difficult to rule out this type of non-normality from the effect sizes alone, a well-fitting mixture does not by itself show that the data-generating process consists of discrete clusters [74].

Moreover, even when effect sizes genuinely arise from a mixture of normals, the reason for the mixture may not be recoverable from coded study characteristics. Distinct components need not reflect a single categorical moderator; they could equally result from several interacting or nonlinear moderators, from continuous moderators whose values cluster across studies, or from combinations of methodological characteristics such as measurement, study quality, or sampling differences, many of which may be uncoded or difficult to code. For these reasons, MetaMix is best regarded as a hypothesis-generating tool for exploring latent heterogeneity structures rather than a direct way of uncovering hidden moderators. Associations between cluster membership and study characteristics can then be tested in targeted follow-up experiments.

Importantly, these limitations concern only the substantive interpretation of the components: the benefits of mixture modelling for publication bias adjustment do not depend on the components being substantively meaningful, only on the mixture describing the distribution of effect sizes better than a single normal. Simulation 3 shows that even when data come from a lognormal distribution rather than a mixture of normals, MetaMix improves adjustment for publication bias relative to standard methods.

Identifiability

Latent heterogeneity and publication bias can produce similar patterns in observed effect sizes, such as asymmetry or an excess of significant results [75], raising the question of how to disentangle the two when both are modelled simultaneously. In MetaMix, identification rests on the different functional forms of the two processes. Selection is modelled as a step function of the p-value and therefore produces discontinuities in the distribution of z-values at the cutoffs, whereas mixture components are smooth in the effect size and cannot produce such a discontinuity (which is why model fit is best inspected on the z-scale, Figure 10).

However, mixture weights and relative publication probabilities can only be separately identified in this way if at least one cluster contains studies spanning different selection probabilities (e.g., both significant and non-significant results). In practice, this is likely the case most of the time, given that the primary studies within each cluster are more dispersed than the true effect sizes, due to sampling variability. However, in settings with very narrow mixture components and large primary-study sample sizes, it is conceivable that one component contains almost entirely significant results while another contains almost entirely non-significant results. In such cases, mixture weights and selection probabilities are not separately identifiable, and strong assumptions for either the selection probabilities or the mixing weights would be required to estimate the model. This failure mode is visible in Simulation 2, where MetaMix occasionally provided evidence against publication bias under two-sided selection with widely separated, narrow clusters (Figure C1).

A second identifiability issue concerns the mixture itself. The ordering constraint on the component means rules out label switching, but the posterior can still be multimodal as different combinations of means and heterogeneities can approximate the data. When fitting models in a Bayesian framework, multimodality is easily detected if different chains settle in different modes, causing convergence warnings, such as very high R values (see [70]). Multimodality can be addressed by initialising the chains in each local maximum. If one maximum clearly dominates (i.e., the data are much more likely under one of the maxima), the inference can be conditioned on that maximum. If not, uncertainty about the correct mode needs to be transparently stated and propagated to all downstream analyses (e.g., via model-averaging or by reporting results according to both identified modes).

Further, I recommend fitting models with a large number of chains and dispersed starting values to be likely to identify multiple maxima if they are present. Of course, as with any mixture model, there is no formal guarantee that all modes have been found, since a mode can have a small basin of attraction; running many chains from dispersed starting values makes a consequential omission unlikely but cannot rule it out [76]. Detailed guidance on addressing multimodality is available at https://maxmaier42.github.io/metamix/articles/multimodality.html.

Future Directions

In principle, meta-analytic mixture modelling could be combined with various other typical meta-analytic models, such as three-level meta-analysis to account for effect size dependencies (e.g., when some primary studies contribute multiple effect sizes or when multiple treatments share a control condition), or additional models of the publication process, such as methods based on the relationship between effect sizes and standard errors ( [51, 53, 77], but see [78]), or different types of selection models [e.g., 79].

Another promising direction is combining mixture modelling with moderator analysis. Moderator analysis, in which researchers specify the factors they expect to influence the effect size in advance, can be considered the theory-driven counterpart to meta-analytic mixture modelling. Combining the two approaches in a single model would allow the mixtures to specifically capture additional patterns in the data that are not yet explained by existing moderators, analogous to fitting a mixture model on the residuals after moderator analysis has been conducted. This approach would allow researchers to directly test whether, after accounting for suitable moderators, residuals are normally distributed, or additional clusters can be found through mixture modelling.

Finally, the currently implemented approach requires model selection between the different meta-analytic models that can be specified in terms of both the number of mixture components and the different models of publication bias. To accommodate uncertainty about the data-generating process, researchers can combine meta-analytic mixture modelling with Bayesian model-averaging [80] [81] [82] [83]. Researchers interested in using model-averaging can do so within the current R-package by mixing the posterior distributions from different models (e.g., with different publication processes) weighted by their posterior probability. Bayesian model-averaging for meta-analytic mixture modelling raises 1) theoretical questions around how to interpret the assignment of primary studies to mixture components when averaging over mixtures with different numbers of components, and 2) practical limitations, as it would vastly increase the time required to fit the models and increase the probability of convergence issues in the larger set of models under consideration for model-averaging.

Concluding Comments

Ultimately, the value of meta-analysis lies not in producing a single summary estimate, but in helping researchers make sense of the heterogeneity across studies and generate hypotheses about which effects apply for whom and under what conditions. By allowing meta-analysts to go beyond the traditional normal-normal framework, meta-analytic mixture modelling is an important step toward better addressing heterogeneity in meta-analysis.

Use of Generative AI

Generative AI (Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Opus 4.7 and Opus 4.6) has been used for minor language editing and to aid with writing code mostly for visualizations and robustness checks.

Effective Sample Size (min ESS) > 500 with the exception of the 4-component random-effects mixture (ESS = 438); however, this model received almost no support from the data (see Model Comparison section).

Model Comparison.

Table 1 reports posterior probabilities for one-to five-component selection mixtures and their non-adjusted (random-effects) counterparts.

Models without publication-bias adjustment received essentially zero posterior probability, indicating overwhelming evidence of publication bias. Among selection mixtures, probability split between three components (0.53) and four (0.42), with five at 0.05 and one/two essentially zero; we report the three-component model in the main text and the four-component model, which splits the near-null cluster in two, in Appendix F. [2%, 26%] of conducted studies but 20% [6%, 46%] of published ones (Table 2).

We next compare the robustness of our results when the 4-component fit, which received 42% of the posterior probability, is used for inference (Appendix F). The 4-mixture split the near-null component into two µ = 0.00 and 0.07, while the components with small and large effects were essentially unchanged (µ = 0.26 and 0.75). The relative publication probabilities were also similar under the two models (0.08 and 0.21 under four components versus 0.09 and 0.25 under three).

Robustness.

We refitted all models under five alternative prior specifications: an inverse-gamma prior on heterogeneities; a lognormal prior on gaps between adjacent component means, alone and combined with the inverse-gamma prior; and narrower and wider half-normal priors on heterogeneities. We further assessed robustness to randomly removing 10% of effect sizes ten times (Appendix F). Across all variations, the one-and two-component models received negligible probability. Component means and heterogeneities were stable throughout, with the main exception being that tighter priors on the heterogeneity lead to a larger µ 3 , (µ3 = 0.93 [0.42, 1.19] under τ ∼ Normal + (0, 0.1) versus 0.59 [0.18, 1.07] under τ ∼ Normal + (0, 0.5)). Relative publication probabilities varied little across variations, and the three-or four-component mixture with publication bias was always selected.

Characterising the components.

We characterised components using the study characteristics of effect sizes with posterior allocation probability above .5 for a given component (Figure 11); restricting to above .75 gave the same picture (Appendix F). The large-effect component consisted mostly of structure-based nudges, particularly default interventions; intervention domain differed little across components.

Appendix A Example Report

In this appendix, I illustrate how to report a meta-analytic mixture analysis, using the nudging data of Mertens et al. [28] analysed in the main text. In practice, this section might follow a section applying linear or machine learning-based moderator analysis [9, 11], unless the moderators already reduced heterogeneity to close to zero. For general reporting guidelines, see Moher et al. [84] (meta-analyses) and Van Doorn et al. [85] (Bayesian analyses). Note that the last section 'Characterising the Components' would be expected to be considerably longer in an empirical paper, where researchers can use their domain expertise to interpret the studies within each component.

Mixture Model

Model Specification, Fitting, and Diagnostics. All models were fitted with the metamixr R-package (version 0.1.0) using rstan [86]; marginal likelihoods were estimated with bridgesampling [87]. We specified the selection model with cutoffs at one-sided p = .5 and p = .975, assuming that effects in the predicted direction are more likely to be published than backfire effects and that significant p-values on two-sided tests are more likely to be published than non-significant p-values. We used the package's default priors: µ m ∼ Normal(0, 1) on component means, τ m ∼ Normal + (0, 0.2) on heterogeneities, Dirichlet(1, . . . , 1) on mixing weights, and a cumulative Dirichlet(1, . . . , 1) on relative publication probabilities. For each mixture model, we first ran 16 chains from dispersed starting values to check for multiple posterior modes (see https://maxmaier42.github.io/metamix/articles/multimodality.html for more details on this approach). The one-component and three-to five-component models had a single mode. The two-component selection model had two modes; refitting within each mode showed the data were overwhelmingly more likely under one (posterior probability > 0.99), so we conditioned inference on that mode. Due to the substantial computational cost involved in fitting Bayesian methods, the number of iterations per cell is lower than commonly used in simulations with only frequentist methods. Nevertheless, the simulation took around 15 CPU years to compute on Warwick HPC clusters. I used 336 iterations rather than the 300 in Bartoš et al.[48], as it allowed for full parallel utilisation of the cluster with 48 cores per node.

Figure 10

Figure 10 compares posterior predictive z-value distributions under each model against the observed data. Non-adjusted mixtures under-predicted the number of studies just above the two-sided significance threshold (z = 1.96); selection mixtures reproduced this discontinuity. Adding components improved fit, with three and four components fitting best; however, some misfit remained for z between 0 and 1.96. Estimates under the selected models. Under the three-component selection mixture, the first component captured null/near-null effects (µ1 = 0.01, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.04]; τ1 = 0.03, [0.00, 0.05]); the second, small effects (µ2 = 0.21, [0.05, 0.34]; τ² = 0.14, [0.02, 0.24]); the third, larger and more heterogeneous effects (µ3 = 0.69, [0.21, 1.13]; τ3 = 0.34, [0.16, 0.49]). Relative to significant studies, non-significant studies in the expected direction were published with probability 0.25 [0.15, 0.37], and those in the unexpected direction with probability 0.09 [0.04, 0.18]. After accounting for selection, the null component was estimated to contain 62% [37%, 77%] of all conducted studies but only 41% [20%, 55%] of published studies, while the large-effect component contained 9%
